title: When Should Indoor Air Quality Be Tested?
h1: When Should You Have Your Indoor Air Quality Tested?
description: Test indoor air quality after water damage, when you notice odors or symptoms, after a remodel or wildfire smoke, or when buying a home. Here's what to know.
quick_answer: Consider testing indoor air quality when you notice musty odors, visible mold or symptoms that improve when you leave the house, after water damage, a remodel or wildfire smoke, and when you buy or move into a home. Every home also needs working carbon monoxide alarms, since CO can't be seen or smelled.
body:
Indoor air quality is hard to judge by feel. Some problems are obvious, like a musty smell. Others, like fine particles or gases from new furniture, aren't noticeable at all. Testing gives you real information so you can fix the actual problem instead of guessing.

What are the signs your indoor air needs attention?

  • Musty or stale odors that don't go away
  • Visible mold on walls, ceilings, windows or around vents
  • Allergy or asthma symptoms that are worse at home and better when you're away
  • Frequent headaches, fatigue or irritated eyes indoors
  • Dust that builds up quickly after cleaning
  • Condensation on windows or damp spots on walls
  • Rooms that feel stuffy or stale

If you notice these, it's a good time to look more closely at the air in your home.

When is testing most useful?

After water damage

Roof leaks, plumbing leaks, a clogged AC drain or a flooded laundry room can lead to hidden mold. Testing after the leak is fixed helps confirm whether growth is a concern behind walls, under floors or in the ductwork.

After a remodel

Drywall dust, paint, adhesives, new cabinets and flooring can release particles and volatile organic compounds, often called VOCs. Testing can show whether levels have settled down.

After wildfire smoke

Smoke particles can get into homes through gaps and HVAC systems, and the smell can linger. Particle monitoring helps you see whether your filtration is keeping up during smoke events.

When buying or moving into a home

You don't know how the previous owners lived, whether they smoked or had pets, or whether there were past leaks or rodent issues in the attic. A baseline check is a smart step before you settle in.

When someone has health concerns

If a family member has asthma, allergies or a new baby is coming, it's reasonable to want to know what's in the air. Talk to your doctor about symptoms, and use testing to look for possible triggers at home.

What can be tested?

  • Particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10): fine dust and smoke particles
  • Humidity: high levels encourage mold and dust mites, low levels cause dryness
  • Carbon dioxide: a sign of how well your home is ventilated
  • VOCs: gases from cleaners, paints, furniture and building materials
  • Mold: air or surface sampling, usually analyzed by a lab
  • Carbon monoxide: from gas appliances, attached garages or blocked vents

Consumer air quality monitors can track particles, humidity, CO2 and VOCs over time, which is useful for spotting patterns. Mold sampling usually requires a specialist and lab analysis.

What about carbon monoxide?

Carbon monoxide is different from other air quality issues because it can be deadly. California requires CO alarms in homes with gas appliances, fireplaces or attached garages. Test them monthly and replace them according to the manufacturer's instructions. If a CO alarm goes off, get everyone outside right away and call 911. If you smell gas, leave the house and call the gas utility from outside.

Can you test indoor air quality yourself?

You can do a lot on your own. A home air monitor shows particle levels, humidity, CO2 and VOCs, and many connect to a phone app so you can see trends. Watch what happens when you cook, run the dryer, open windows or when smoke rolls in. A simple hygrometer tells you if humidity is in the 30 to 50 percent range. And a flashlight check of the attic, under sinks and around the furnace can reveal leaks, droppings or dust buildup. If you find mold or suspect a hidden problem, bring in a professional.

What should you do with the results?

Testing only helps if it leads to a fix. Common improvements include:

  1. Upgrading to a better HVAC filter that fits snugly
  2. Fixing leaky return ducts that pull in attic or garage air
  3. Cleaning ducts after a remodel, smoke event or rodent problem
  4. Adding a whole-home air purifier, UV light, dehumidifier or humidifier
  5. Improving ventilation with bathroom and kitchen exhaust fans
  6. Repairing leaks and drying out damp areas

faqs: How often should I check my indoor air quality?
A continuous home air monitor lets you see changes as they happen. Beyond that, check after major events like leaks, remodels or smoke, and whenever you notice new odors or symptoms.
Are home air quality monitors accurate?

Quality consumer monitors are good at showing trends in particles, humidity and CO2. They're less precise than professional equipment, and they don't replace a working carbon monoxide alarm or a lab test for mold.
Can my HVAC system make indoor air quality worse?
It can if the filter is dirty or the wrong size, if the ducts are leaky or dirty, or if there's moisture around the coil. A well-maintained system with a good filter usually helps air quality.
Does wildfire smoke get inside my home?

Yes, fine smoke particles can get in through gaps around doors and windows and through leaky ducts. Keep windows closed, run the HVAC fan with a MERV 13 filter if your system can handle it, and consider a portable air purifier.
